Abstract
Model-based stationing refers to the process of registering a set of measurements to a model. Speciﬁcally, in the surveying
context, this refers to the process of determining the station, i.e., the position and orientation, of a total station given a
user-provided building ﬂoor plan and a series of polar measurements. Traditional methods compute the station using a set of
known control points. We propose an automatic workﬂow which uses a novel registration method that does not require any
known control points in order to ﬁnd the station with high accuracy. Our registration algorithm relies on angle and distance
measurements only; therefore, it is not limited to modern image-assisted total stations. In addition, the proposed workﬂow
comprises a modeling phase to deal with model inaccuracies and produces reliable and accurate results. Quantitative and
qualitative tests on synthetic and real-world scenarios demonstrate the performance and robustness of our automatic workﬂow
and registration method.
Keywords Registration · Model-based stationing · Automated workﬂow · Robotic total station · Robot control
1 Introduction
A robotic total station (RTS) is an instrument used in sur-
veying tasks capable of measuring angles and distances
electronically with very high accuracy. Common indoor
applications of an RTS include laying out mechanical or
electrical components, HVAC (Heating, Ventilation, and Air
Conditioning)installations,ordrywalls.Anothersetofappli-
cations consists of quality control tasks such as ﬁre stop
documentation and as-designed versus as-built comparison.
Having the ability to determine the station, i.e., the position
and orientation of an RTS with high accuracy is imperative
for these applications.

1.1 Problem Formulation
Traditional stationing methods such as free stationing, trian-
gulation, and trilateration rely on control points to compute
the station of an RTS with high accuracy [23, 35, 38]. A
control point is a permanent reference which should not be
disturbed and should be clearly visible. Its coordinates in
space must be included in the building ﬂoor plan (model) to
allow the stationing of an RTS. Usually, control points are
established using reﬂective targets, prisms, or features such
as building corners.
These methods achieve high accuracy with only a few
control points (2–5), however, maintaining undisturbed and
clearly visible control points in indoor environments is usu-
ally not practical in the long term. It takes a considerable
amount of time and costs to set up and maintain them in
place. In addition, during the stationing process, the user
is responsible for providing the correspondences that relate
the control points in the model to their corresponding mea-
surements in the environment, thus making the stationing
procedure tedious and prone to errors.
In the surveying context, there also exist methods for pose
estimation that do not require control points. These methods
solve the correspondence problem and the pose estimation
simultaneously [5, 20, 30]. Most of them are based on dense

Apart from theoretical feasibility considerations, the most

risk of inducing serious consequences and damage due to

repeatability and robustness are essential in any surveying
task. Because of the high stake at play, solutions relying on
automatic feature detection and correspondences [28, 31] are
merely of academic relevance for the task at hand, rather than
practical suitability, as they can deliver a certain outcome nei-
ther at the required robustness, repeatability, nor accuracy,
resulting in serious concerns and liability issues in case of
failure.
1.2 Contribution
We propose an automatic model-based stationing algorithm
for indoor applications when no control points are available
and high accuracy is required using a small set of mea-
surements. There are two main motivations for the design
of our approach, namely (a) to reduce user-induced errors
by minimizing user interaction overall and (b) to increase
the stationing repeatability. In contrast to classical stationing
methods, where the user is responsible for measuring the con-
trolpointsandassigningitscorrespondencestothemodel,the
proposedalgorithmautomaticallydeterminestheappropriate
places in the room to take distance measurements to achieve
high stationing accuracy. This reduces the user interaction
with the RTS, thus minimizing user-induced errors. Besides,
our algorithm eliminates the requisite to keep undisturbed
and clearly visible control points.
Our approach consists of two stages for fast and reliable
stationing. The ﬁrst stage consists of doing a 360◦quick scan
of the room and a coarse estimation of the station of the
RTS. The second step comprises a 360◦stop-and-go scan of
the room and a ﬁne estimation of the station of the RTS. To
perform the coarse and ﬁne estimations, we introduce a novel
robustregistrationmethodcapableofregisteringasetofpolar
measurements in a 2D ﬂoor plan. Our registration method can
cope with up to 40% of outliers and partial occlusions and
does not need a manual assignment of the correspondences
between the measurements and the ﬂoor plan segments.
Furthermore, we introduce a proportional controller to
collect distance measurements at a constant height. This con-
troller helps us avoid taking distance measurements on the
ﬂoor or ceiling of the room during the 360◦quick scan. This
is required because the pose of the RTS with respect to the
outer environment is not known in advance and, it can be
arbitrarily chosen by the operator. For example, an operator
may decide to take distance measurements close to the ceil-
ing of the room to avoid obstacles like openings or furniture.
Since a 2D ﬂoor plan of a room only includes information
about the walls of the room, taking measurements on the ﬂoor
or ceiling would hinder our registration algorithm.
The proposed workﬂow also includes a modeling phase
to deal with as-designed model inaccuracies. Construction
work is never exactly built as-designed and often ﬂoor plans
are not updated during the construction process. Even if
updated, we have to expect modeling errors that do not allow
a high stationing accuracy. Therefore, the proposed workﬂow
includes an as-built ﬂoor plan estimation phase to increase
the robustness and reach high stationing repeatability.
We present a series of simulations and real-world tests
showing that our automatic model-based stationing workﬂow
achieves high accuracy. The main contributions of our work
are as therefore as follows:
1. An automatic model-based stationing workﬂow which
simpliﬁes the stationing process in indoor environments
when no control points are available.
2. A registration method for robust coarse stationing and
accurate ﬁne stationing.
3. A 360◦scanning method to collect measurements at a
constant height.
4. A modeling method designed to cope with the inaccura-
cies of as-designed ﬂoor plan models.
2 Related Work
Our work is mainly concerned with the stationing of an
RTS, automated geometric modeling and real time robot con-
trol. In the following, we outline registration methods which
solve pose estimation without known correspondences and
methods that solve the registration given a set of correspon-
dences. Since we cannot expect that the as-designed model
is accurate, we also review methods for model creation and
geometry checks from laser data. Since we seek to apply a
correction to the RTS based on an error value, we touch on
methods to control robotic systems in real time, as well. Note
that there is basically no dedicated literature that combines
the model creation and stationing step, as proposed in the
present manuscript.

2.1 Registration Methods
Resection (or free stationing), triangulation, and trilateration
are well-known methods used to determine the station of sur-
veying instruments like RTS. Many trilateration methods for
indoor localization leverage received signal strength indica-
tion (RSSI) data [41]. RSSI-based methods must cope with
the interference and noise in the signals, to reduce the local-
ization error rate [7, 40]. Although not directly related to
our work, these methods can be applied to locate an RTS in
indoor environments, since they can provide high accuracy
in static measurement scenarios.
The Helmert transformation [8] is a method used to ﬁnd
the similarity transformation that aligns two sets of points.
Methods based on singular value decomposition (SVD) can
also be used to ﬁnd the transformation that aligns two sets of
corresponding points [3, 19, 37].
There also exist least-squares methods that solve the pose
from point-to-point, point-to-line, and point-to-plane corre-
spondences. Zhou et al. [42] show that their algorithm is
stable and accurate even when the number of correspon-
dences is small. Malis [29] developed an algorithm that
utilizes the “h-resultant” method; which is not only accurate
and robust, but also computationally efﬁcient.
The aforementioned methods could be applied to the
pose estimation of an RTS from point-to-line correspon-
dences. Removing thus the necessity to maintain surveyed
control points. Nevertheless, the user would still need to
assign the correspondences between the measurements and
the ﬂoor plan segments in the model. In this work we are
concerned with the workﬂow automation in order to reduce
the user workload, which in turn aims to reduce user-induced
error. Therefore, we developed a registration method which
does not need a manual assignment of the correspondences
between the measurements and the ﬂoor plan segments.
Klug et al. [25] developed a semi-automatic user-guided
workﬂow to register an RTS with a 3D CAD model in indoor
environments without control points. The user interaction of
their system is reduced to selecting a Manhattan-like cor-
ner structure for initial model alignment. Their approach is
closely related to the system proposed by Bosché [4] but
is designed for RTS registration. In contrast, we propose
a two-stage workﬂow for automatic registration of an RTS
within a polygonal model. This model may be extracted from
a CAD model, and we do not require any known control
points as well.
Stapleton et al. [34] developed an algorithm based on
the generalized Hough transform to compute a coarse pose
estimation. Subsequently, they reﬁne the estimate using the
iterative method proposed by Srivatsan et al. [33]. They also
designed a sampling strategy, learned through reinforcement
learning, to effectively sample indoor environments. In con-
trast, we employ a two-phase sampling strategy to obtain
uniformly distributed measurements around the RTS. Hore-
muž and Andersson [17] suggest measuring 10–30 points
distributed around the RTS in a half circle. Later, Horemuž
and Jansson [18] showed that placing the RTS in or near the
center of gravity of the measured points is the best if the goal
is to determine the pose of the RTS as precisely as possible.
2.2 Automated Modeling and Geometry Check
Recently, many methods have been developed for accurate
generation of geometric models [22, 24, 39]. They are used
for condition assessment, progress tracking, and documenta-
tion of civil infrastructure systems etc. Although there exist
many technologies for point data collection, these methods
often use observations from terrestrial laser scanning to gen-
erate accurate geometric models.
Jung et al. [21] propose a method for automated geomet-
ric modeling of indoor structures. They used a constrained
least squares method to create an as-built building informa-
tion model (BIM) of the interior of the building. By enforcing
coplanarityandorthonormalityconstraints,theyproducereg-
ularized models, i.e., models which walls, ﬂoors, etc., are
composed of straight lines, either parallel or orthogonal.
Although we also use a least-squares approach to model
indoor environments, we do not enforce orthonormality con-
straints, since we found that interior walls are often far from
being orthogonal to one another.
Honti et al. [16] developed a method to perform an auto-
mated geometry check. They perform a plane segmentation
to compare a single plane with the model data. Then, they
quantiﬁed the wall ﬂatness by measuring the deviations for
each measured point and showing them as a heat map.
Esfahani et al. [9] investigated in a systematic and quan-
titative way what modeling errors to expect in different
scenarios. They investigated the variances and inaccura-
cies from manual and semi-automated modeling for typical
indoor scenarios, as discussed in our work. In addition, the
impactofusertrainingwasstudied.Untraineduserscanreach
an average absolute error between 2cm and 6cm by manually
ﬁtting walls to point clouds. Trained users are able to reduce
this error to less than 2cm. They show that the usage of semi-
automated software packages that apply iterative algorithms
such as RANSAC [10] did not signiﬁcantly reduce this error.
2.3 Real Time Proportional Controllers
Proportional integral derivative (PID) controllers are widely
used to stabilize robotic systems which are subject to external
disturbances [2] and need to track targets under dynamic
conditions [1, 6].
An RTS is an instrument that must not be perturbed under
any circumstances during a surveying task. Consequently, we
do not have to deal with any external disturbances. Moreover,

Control-point Stationing
The steps to determine the station of an RTS using control
points include (see left of Fig. 3): (a) placing and setting up
the RTS in the known environment, (b) loading the model on
the controller, (c) measuring the control points, (d) assign-
ing the correspondences between the measurements and the
model control points, and (e) calculating the pose of the RTS
in the coordinate system of the model control points.
When using control points to determine the station, the
user is responsible for measuring the control points and
assigning its correspondences to the model. A minimum of
two control points are required to compute the station, while
a larger number is advisable in practice to achieve higher
accuracy. Given the correspondences of the control points
and the measurements, the pose estimation problem can be
solved using the least squares method [8], for example.
The stationing based on control points demands a high
level of user interaction, i.e., measuring control points, and
assigning correspondences. These tasks require the oper-
ator’s full attention at all times throughout the stationing

4 Automatic Model-based Stationing
Our proposed workﬂow is shown on the right of Fig. 3. In
contrast to CPS, our workﬂow requires the user to provide
input information only at the beginning of the stationing pro-
cess. This input is used for disambiguation when there exists
a rotational symmetry in the model, as it is impossible to give
a unique solution in rooms with the shape of, for example, a
rectangle. The user only has to indicate the ID of the wall to
which the RTS initially points to. This ID is obtained from the
loaded ﬂoor plan and is already sufﬁcient for the stationing
process. Because we collect this information in advance, the
operator can start the process and move on with other tasks
until the stationing process is complete.
In practical scenarios, the as-designed ﬂoor plan might not
ﬁt the actual layout of the room, making its registration to
measurements a challenging problem. To solve this problem,
we estimate an as-built ﬂoor plan during the proposed sta-
tioning process. To relate the as-built and as-designed ﬂoor
plans, we use a wall and a corner of both ﬂoor plans to align
them and register them in the same coordinate system. The
user can therefore choose on the controller the wall and cor-
ner of the room that are used to align the ﬂoor plans. Note
that the estimation of the as-built ﬂoor plan is an optional
task. It is necessary to estimate it only when it has never
been estimated before, or it was created a long time ago, for
example.
Further following the illustration on the right of Fig. 3, the
core of the proposed workﬂow consists of two 360◦scans of
the room and a coarse-to-ﬁne estimation of the RTS’s station.
The ﬁrst 360◦quick scan is followed by a coarse estimate
of the RTS’s station. After that, the controller performs an
estimation of inliers, and computes the sampling spots where
the RTS is supposed to take new measurements. The second
360◦stop-and-go scan allows us to do a ﬁne estimation of
the RTS’s station based on stationary measurements of high
accuracy. Based on the user option, the controller estimates
and aligns the as-built ﬂoor plan. As a ﬁnal step, the controller
performs the ﬁne stationing procedure, i.e., calculating the
ﬁnal station.
Note that the proposed registration method estimates the
2D pose of the RTS w.r.t.a 2D ﬂoor plan. The 2D pose of
the instrument is enough for surveying tasks like layouting
on the ceiling or ﬂoor, i.e., marking points, lines and curves
to indicate areas where to drill or anchor components [26,
27]. In case the 3D pose of the instrument is required for
layouting on the walls, for example, the user can point the
EDM to the ﬂoor or the ceiling and take an observation to
estimate the height of the RTS (see Section 3).

Inlier observations are used to determine good sampling
spots for the stop-and-go scan. To obtain uniformly dis-
tributed observations around the RTS we use (a) nes equally
spaced sampling spots, with nes ≪N, being N the number
of observations, or (b) n ps sampling spots per segment, with

plan (see Fig. 7c). The criteria for selecting between these
two strategies depends on the layout of the room. For rooms
where the length of all the walls is approximately the same,
both options work well, but the ﬁrst option is particularly use-
ful for rooms where some walls are signiﬁcantly shorter, or
longer, than the others. We use the second option by default,
but the user can change it if considered necessary.
Since the RTS stops before taking a new measurement
and we know the correspondences, we only need to capture a
small set of observations (<30) to compute the station of the
RTS with high accuracy. In addition, during our experiments
with real-world scenarios, we observed that completing the
stop-and-go scan using all possible sampling spots takes ×10
the time needed to complete the quick scan (approximately
ten minutes). Therefore, we use less than 30 sampling points.
To estimate nes equally spaced sampling spots, we sim-
ply calculate the 2D coordinates of nes equally spaced points
in the ﬂoor plan, and we select as sampling spots the 2D
coordinates of the nearest registered inlier observations.
Alternatively, to estimate n ps sampling spots per segment,
we calculate the 2D coordinates of n ps equally spaced points
in each segment of the ﬂoor plan, and we select as sam-
pling spots the 2D coordinates of the nearest registered inlier
observations.
The main argument in defense of using two separate scans
is that it is impractical to do a single 360◦stop-and-go scan.
Our proposed workﬂow relies only on angle and distance
measurements. To compute the station with a single 360◦
scan, we would need to simultaneously infer good sampling
spots and take measurements. Good sampling spots could
be inferred considering imagery acquired with a visible light
(RGB) camera to avoid taking measurements on openings
(e.g., windows, open doors) or furniture. However, this would
constrain the application of our workﬂow to image-assisted
total stations. Therefore, we use the coarse station to estimate
good sampling spots in the room for a subsequent efﬁcient
stop-and-go scan.

4.4 Fine Stationing
At the end of our workﬂow we compute the station of the
RTS using the observations obtained during the stop-and-
go scan and their correspondences. To do so, we use our
proposed FreePolygon algorithm. Our registration method is
capable of computing the station of an RTS with or without
correspondences. However, the computation of the station is
faster using correspondences. Besides, our method can cope
with up to 40% of outliers and partial occlusions. The details
of the algorithm are discussed in Section 5.
The coarse estimation of the station gives us a good
approximation of the RTS’s pose (see Section 4.1). However,
such an estimation is not accurate enough to perform any
surveying task. Therefore, in order to achieve higher accu-
racy, we employ the observation-to-wall correspondences
we obtain during the inliers estimation (see Section 4.2),
alongside the observations, to carry out a ﬁne estimation of
the RTS’s station. Because construction work is never built
exactly as-designed, we use the as-built ﬂoor plan to esti-
mate the RTS’s station, thus ensuring robustness and high
stationing repeatability.

proposed algorithm achieves high stationing accuracy with
reasonable modeling errors.
7 Discussion and Conclusion
In this work, we proposed a new algorithm to estimate the
station of an RTS in indoor environments. The major advan-
tages of our approach are
• the high repeatability of the stationing without the need
to maintain surveyed control points,
• the avoidance of user-induced errors by minimizing the
user interaction and,
• the new-gained possibility for operators to conduct dif-
ferent tasks during the automatic process.
Our experiments show that the proposed ABMS delivers
equivalent results to the gold-standard CPS method, while
no further user involvement is required.

Our workﬂow incorporates several automatic tasks to
reduce the user interaction with the RTS, with the aim of
minimizing user-induced errors. In addition, it includes fea-
tures such as a proportional height controller and a modeling
phase to increase the robustness and accuracy of stationing,
and to reduce the time required to calculate the station of an
RTS. To the best of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst approach to
fully automate the stationing process and to allow the oper-
ator during the stationing process to conduct other related
tasks.
In the following, we quickly discuss several aspects con-
cerning our current workﬂow and potential improvements
for future work. Note that the plausibility of some proposed
changes strongly depends on further potential iterations
concerning hardware development and the availability of
particular hardware features, while certain limitations are
naturally given by physics (e.g., speed and accuracy of servo
movements, travel time of laser light and according measure-
ment timings).
Proportional controllers in quick scanning Laser meters, or
EDM, are designed to take distance measurements while
being static. In our case, the RTS continuously rotates during
the quick scan, which reduces the accuracy of the distance
measurements and, the faster the RTS rotates, the less precise
the EDM measurements become. This means that the overall
scanning speed is clearly a trade-off between usability, i.e.,
time to ﬁnish, and accuracy.
Right now the RTS rotates at a constant speed while doing
the quick scan (e.g., 5deg/sec). We opted for a simplistic
proportional controller for correcting the height, because it
can easily cope with the expected changes at this rotation
speed. Of course, there is room to use a more evolved con-
troller. We can also further improve the quick scan routine

world scenarios in which we tested the proposed workﬂow
are convex. Methods utilizing terrestrial laser scanning are
preferred [21, 22] to create a model in non-convex build-

Our rather simple modeling method is especially useful for
surveying tasks such as laying out mechanical or electrical
components, installation of dry walls, etc. Before placing dry
walls, most of the building interiors resemble empty, box-like
structures. Albeit challenging, improving this aspect of our
workﬂow would signiﬁcantly increase the range of environ-

Abstract: Model-based stationing refers to the process of registering a set of measurements to a model. Speciﬁcally, in the surveying context, this refers to the process of determining the station, i.e., the position and orientation, of a total station given a user-provided building ﬂoor plan and a series of polar measurements. Traditional methods compute the station using a set of known control points. We propose an automatic workﬂow which uses a novel registration method that does not require any known control points in order to ﬁnd the station with high accuracy. Our registration algorithm relies on angle and distance measurements only; therefore, it is not limited to modern image-assisted total stations. In addition, the proposed workﬂow comprises a modeling phase to deal with model inaccuracies and produces reliable and accurate results. Quantitative and qualitative tests on synthetic and real-world scenarios demonstrate the performance and robustness of our automatic workﬂow and registration method.
